PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. The Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide (VIG).
Voter Initiative Process. California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional amendments through the statewide initiative process. Supporters of an initiative collect signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot. State law sets how many valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot. Supporters notify the Secretary of State once they have gathered 25 percent of the necessary signatures.
Special Taxes. State taxes can be raised by the Legislature or by voters. When a “special tax” is created, the revenue from that tax is dedicated to a specific purpose or program. For example, certain fuel taxes can only be used to pay for public roads and other transportation programs.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments follow the law, use money, and run their programs. These reviews are called audits. An audit may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly over time while other audits are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process. This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit. If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor’s summary to be included in the VIG. If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.
Ongoing Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From New or Increased Special Taxes. Proposition 41 also requires the State Auditor to periodically review programs that receive funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026. These ongoing audits would happen every four years. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor will include in these audits, including recommendations to improve program efficiency. Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of this ongoing work will be paid using the new tax revenue.
State Appropriations Limit. The State Constitution limits how much tax revenues the state can spend each year. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes and special taxes. However, certain types of spending, for example for infrastructure, are excluded from this limit. Under Proposition 41, the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the limit.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Auditor Costs, Mostly Paid by New Revenues. Proposition 41 would increase State Auditor costs by creating new and ongoing audit requirements. The costs would depend on (1) the number of new or increased special taxes that are proposed and approved and (2) the complexity of the programs being audited. These costs likely would be in the range of the low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time. The one-time and ongoing audit costs associated with special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature would be paid from the revenues collected by the special taxes. One-time audit costs associated with special taxes that do not ultimately appear on the ballot or are rejected by voters would be paid from the state’s General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. Proposition 41 would require a summary of the State Auditor’s review to appear in the VIG when a voter initiative with a special tax appears on the ballot. These audit summaries could add several pages to the VIG, which would increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Possible Savings if State Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to make recommendations for programs to reduce costs or improve efficiency. Proposition 41 could result in savings or improved services if policymakers implement the State Auditor’s recommendations and those recommendations prove effective. Any resulting savings would depend on future decisions and are not known.
Net Effect Not Known. The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 41
CALIFORNIANS DESERVE BETTER RESULTS FOR OUR TAX DOLLARS
Prop. 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct independent public audits of programs funded by proposed new taxes in order to increase transparency and accountability and drive better outcomes.
Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country-on top of our high cost of living. This year alone, California’s state government will spend more than $350 billion-a 79% increase in spending since 2019. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it.
We deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop. 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Here’s how Prop. 41 works.
PUBLIC AUDITS TO PROVIDE ACCOUNTABILITY, TRANSPARENCY AND OVERSIGHT
Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct performance and financial audits of the programs funded by new tax measures, with the results posted publicly. The audits must:
• Track all program spending and assess whether it’s achieving its intended outcomes; • Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability; • Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; • Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and programs made more effective.
Prop. 41 requires audits both before taxes are voted on to provide transparency to voters, and ongoing audits of programs funded by approved taxes to ensure accountability. PROP. 41: INDEPENDENT, PUBLIC INFORMATION FOR VOTERS ON PROPOSED TAXES
Before we vote on new taxes to fund programs, voters should have access to independent information about how those programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding. Under Prop. 41, the Auditor’s findings must be posted publicly and in the Voter Information Guide-so voters can make informed decisions about new taxes without having to rely on information from special interests or politicians.
“This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending- ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. It provides an independent, public report card for government spending, so government programs work better for everyone.” -Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce
PROP. 41: A BETTER DEAL FOR TAXPAYERS
Prop. 41 doesn’t raise taxes-it protects taxpayers’ interests:
• Reduces the waste and fraud that have cost California taxpayers billions of dollars in recent years; • Requires all taxes to comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit-including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Prop. 41 ensures taxpayers get better results-not just a bigger tax bill.
“Every tax dollar we waste is a dollar that could actually help someone. Californians already pay the highest state income and sales taxes in the country-we need better transparency and accountability to make sure our tax dollars produce results. Prop. 41 delivers.” -Steve Westly, former Controller of California.
Please join good government groups, small business owners, accountants, taxpayers and public transparency advocates in voting Yes on 41.
For more information, visit: www.ResultsCA.org
Denise LeDuc Froemming , CPA, President
California Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs)
Tom Hayes , Fmr. California State Auditor
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association (CalTax)
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 41
THIS IS A BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED SMOKE SCREEN
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 41 is not really about audits. This is all a trick so approximately 200 billionaires can keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 41 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 41 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 41 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
To add insult to injury, Prop. 41 isn’t just a scheme, it’s an expensive one-it would cost the state time and money. SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS FUNDED THIS

This is very helpful context. Let me now understand the full picture:

1. **Prop 40** (the "Billionaire Tax"): One-time 5% tax on net worth above $1 billion for those who were CA residents on Jan 1, 2026. Revenue: tens of billions, 90% to healthcare. Its drafters exempted the revenue from the Gann limit (state spending limit) and from school funding requirements (Prop 98). Sponsored by SEIU-UHW. Bernie Sanders supports it.

2. **Prop 41**: Constitutional amendment that (a) nullifies state taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from the state spending limit — this directly targets Prop 40's exemption; (b) requires pre-election audits of programs funded by special tax initiatives; (c) requires ongoing audits every 4 years of programs funded by new/increased special taxes. Funded primarily by Building a Better California (Sergey Brin ~$102 million, plus other tech billionaires). 

3. **Prop 42**: Outlaws retroactive taxation — also a counter to Prop 40 (which taxes wealth as of Dec 31, 2026 for residents as of Jan 1, 2026; if someone moved out, hmm, actually Prop 42 targets the retroactive aspect).

4. **Conflict rule**: If Prop 41 (or 42) gets more yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is blocked from taking effect.

So the real question for the user: how should they vote on Prop 41? The answer depends heavily on their view of Prop 40 and the broader policy considerations. But they asked me to come to a decision. Let me do more research to understand:

- The funding details.

Also, I should consider the merits of the audit provisions independent of the Prop 40 conflict. Some good-government groups might genuinely like performance audits. But the primary purpose seems to be nullifying Prop 40.

Key considerations for my recommendation:

**Arguments FOR Prop 41 (Yes):**
- Transparency/accountability: independent State Auditor reviews of programs funded by new special taxes, before voters vote and every 4 years. This is genuinely a good-government feature. The State Auditor is respected and nonpartisan.
- Taxpayer rebates: revenues above the Gann limit are refunded to taxpayers; including special taxes in the limit honors the voter-approved spending limit from 1979 (Prop 4, Gann limit).
- Could curb waste (e.g., homelessness spending).
- Supported by CalCPAs, CalTax, CalAsian Chamber, Steve Westly (former Controller), former State Auditor Tom Hayes.

**Arguments AGAINST Prop 41 (No):**
- Its primary purpose is to nullify Prop 40, the billionaire tax — it's a countermeasure funded by ~$100M+ from Sergey Brin and other billionaires who would be subject to the wealth tax. It's designed so that even if Prop 40 passes with a majority, Prop 41 (or 42) passing with more votes would kill it.
- The audit timing (at 25% of signatures, before qualification) is odd — it audits programs that don't exist yet, and the "10% cost reduction" requirement biases the analysis toward cuts.
- Subjecting special taxes to the Gann limit could trigger automatic taxpayer refunds rather than spending the money on the intended purpose — meaning new special taxes could effectively force cuts/refunds instead of funding their purpose. That could make any new dedicated tax nearly impossible to implement as intended.
- Cost: low millions per year to the Auditor's office; General Fund pays for audits of taxes that never reach ballot/fail — meaning taxpayers pay to audit measures they rejected.
- It applies retroactively to taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026 (i.e., Prop 40 itself).
- Democratic-aligned groups, SEIU, Bernie Sanders oppose.

Prop
41
CA
Prop
41
|
Constitutional Amendment
Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes.
Requires audits of citizen initiatives for special taxes. Imposes spending limits on all new special taxes.
SPUR's Recommendation
More transparency and accountability in government spending are worthy objectives. However, the Legislative Analyst’s Office and the state auditor already have the authority to evaluate policies and programs to ensure they are equitable and efficient. Prop. 41 was primarily placed on the ballot to defeat Prop. 40, a measure to tax billionaires. In addition, it would constrain local and state governments’ ability to raise revenue now and in the future for much-needed housing, transportation, infrastructure, and social services, which are already facing cuts at the federal and state levels.
Vote NO
What Prop. 41 Would Do
Proposition 41 would require the state auditor, working with the Legislative Analyst’s Office, to conduct an independent review of any state-level citizen initiative that aims to create a new special tax once it reaches 25% of the required signature threshold to be placed on the ballot. (Special taxes differ from general taxes in that they dedicate revenue to a specific purpose.) All new state-level special taxes would be audited every four years.
Additionally, any new special taxes passed after January 1, 2026 — whether proposed through legislation or through voter initiatives — would be subject to the Gann Limit, a voter-imposed revenue spending limit explained in the Backstory section below.
The audit of proposed citizen initiatives would examine the individual programs that would receive funding through the special tax and assess whether the programs are sufficiently cost-efficient in their hiring and operating practices. It would recommend how the programs could save 10% of their costs. The audit information would be included in the voter information guide, which would increase printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per initiative, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
If a special tax passes, the state auditor would be required to conduct audits every four years to assess spending, evaluate efficiency, and recommend improvements. The auditor would consider public input when measuring the program’s effectiveness. The revenues generated would cover implementation costs. However, the state would pay the initial audit cost if voters rejected the special tax.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to the so-called billionaire tax, Prop. 40 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-40-billionaire-tax). If both measures pass, the one receiving more votes would prevail.
The Backstory
Special taxes are taxes whose revenues are dedicated to a specific purpose rather than contributing to the state’s general fund budget. The State Legislature can levy special taxes with two-thirds voter approval, or an initiative placed on the ballot by voter signatures can do so with a simple majority (50% plus one vote). Currently, special taxes have no audit requirements or spending caps.
Since the late 1970s, California has faced numerous tax limitations through Prop. 13 and other constitutional amendments. The Gann Limit imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. If the state’s revenues exceed the Gann Limit — a dollar amount based on the state’s spending level in 1978–1979, adjusted for population and per capita income — half of revenues over the limit must be allocated to K–14 education and the other half returned to taxpayers. 1 Historically, the Gann Limit has rarely affected distribution of the state’s revenues, but if the state experiences strong income gains (including business/corporate/stock gains) over the limit, it could result in decreasing investment in state priorities such as housing, health care, economic development, and infrastructure.
The fiscal impacts of Prop. 41 are unknown. Adding pages to the voter information guide would cost money, but the audits could also create savings. If this measure prevents the state from raising new revenues from future taxes, it could have a significant negative fiscal impact in the longer term.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to Prop. 40, a one-time special tax on individuals with more than $1 billion in assets. Prop. 40 is intended to offset federal funding cuts to critical social safety net programs, including Medi-Cal, CalFresh, and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. The revenues generated from Prop. 40 would be exempt from the Gann Limit.
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot through a signature-gathering effort led by Building a Better California, which is funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. It requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass. If it passes with more votes than Prop. 40, it would nullify Prop. 40. (Building a Better California has also placed Prop. 42 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-42-personal-property-taxes), a separate countermeasure to Prop. 40, on the ballot.)
Equity Impacts
Restricting spending from special taxes could negatively affect efforts to fund health care, food assistance, and other programs that disproportionately benefit lower-income Californians and communities of color.
Pro
Audits of proposed citizen initiatives could help ensure that the programs they would fund are cost-effective.
Cons
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot to prevent a competing measure from succeeding. It could affect the state’s ability to raise revenue from other tax measures in the future.
Applying spending limits to new revenue measures could constrain local and state governments’ ability to fund urgent priorities amid unprecedented federal and state budget cuts.
Vote NO

California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it. Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). “I don’t think that people at this point realize they’re direct countermeasures because there hasn’t been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC. Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect. What each measure does Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7) during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit. Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost. Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42. “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal,” said Megan Jones, a tax attorney with Holland and Knight. The Legislature has tried unsuccessfully in the past to pass multiple wealth taxes (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/tax-pros/law/legislation/2023-2024/AB259-011923.pdf), Jones said. If Prop. 42 passes, she said, it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again in the future. Who’s funding the fights Backers of the billionaire tax — primarily SEIU-UHW — have raised about $31 million to pass the measure, mostly from union coffers. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) also supports the measure. Californians are being asked to vote "yes" or "no" on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office, would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes.

SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known and may be cited as the
Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency
in California Government Act of 2026.
SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
The people of the State of California hereby find and
declare the following:
(a) Every day, Californians are facing an affordability
crisis. Costs for housing, food, electricity, health care,
home and auto insurance, and many other life
necessities continue to escalate.
(b) Californians are already among the highest-taxed
people in the United States. A recent analysis by a
nonpartisan research institute concluded that
California ranks 48th in the nation in subjecting its
population to taxes, when considering individual
income taxes, sales taxes, property taxes, and other
forms of taxation. California has the highest state sales
tax in the nation, the highest top income tax rate, and
the highest tax on gasoline, among other indicators.
(c) Public programs provide much-needed services,
including to children, families, and the most vulnerable
in our state. But billions of our tax dollars have flowed
into programs like homelessness efforts, with far too
little to show for it.
(d) Before asking taxpayers to pay even more of their
hard-earned money to support programs that are
ineffective, we must institute greater transparency and
trackable progress of program improvements to ensure
we stop funding failure and start funding successful
outcomes. Government must use our tax dollars more
wisely.
41 (e) Some of these efforts are already underway. For
example, the Newsom Administration has sought to
increase efficiency in government through greater
utilization of technology and automation, creation of an
Office of Data Innovation, and modernizing the
Department of Motor Vehicles. This is consistent with
earlier efforts President Obama undertook at the
federal level aimed at reducing waste in government
and cutting underperforming programs.
(f) However, while these existing efforts are a good
start, more should be done to reduce inefficiency and
cut government waste. For example, recent studies
have found that as much as 25 cents of every dollar in
some programs are lost to inefficiency or waste.
(g) Nonetheless, the Legislature and special interest
groups continue to propose new and higher taxes for
pet projects without doing the hard work of ensuring
that government programs are already using their
existing revenues as effectively and efficiently as
possible. Californians have a right to require that state
government improve the effectiveness and efficiency of
programs and cut waste before asking us to pay even
higher taxes—which just make our cost-of-living crisis
even worse.
148 | Text of Proposed Laws
(h) In 1979, California’s voters approved a state
spending cap to help check wasteful spending and
encourage more effective government—and to return
any excess revenues above the limit to taxpayers.
However, in the years since, special interests have
repeatedly passed new taxes that exempted
themselves from the state spending limit. This pushes
taxes even higher and makes it less likely that excessive

spiral further out of control before the new efficiency

Even if one opposes Prop 40 itself, many editorial boards (including the LA Times, which also opposes Prop 40) find the countermeasure tactic deceptive.
2. Audit mechanics are problematic:
   - Audits at 25% of signatures, before qualification known — wastes state money auditing measures that never qualify (paid from General Fund).
   - The audit must identify 10% annual savings — a built-in bias.
   - For new programs, audit criteria ("is the program currently acquiring resources at lowest cost") are nonsensical pre-implementation — audit theater.
   - The LAO/State Auditor already have authority to analyze/audit; the LAO already writes impartial analyses for every ballot measure. So the marginal informational value is questionable.
3. Spending-limit provision is far-reaching: any new special tax (even for disaster relief, wildfires, etc.) after Jan 1, 2026 couldn't be exempted from the Gann limit — meaning if the state is at the limit, new tax revenue would have to be rebated rather than spent on its purpose, effectively banning new dedicated funding streams. This constrains future democratic choices by voters themselves (both legislative and initiative special taxes).
4. Retroactive nullification: it applies to taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026, i.e., designed to catch Prop 40 on the same ballot.
5. Editorial consensus: LA Times (Skelton: "twin poison pills... No"), McClatchy boards (Sac Bee et al.: No, "insidious... presented as a good governance measure when it's really about defeating Prop 40"), Press Democrat (No), Bay Area Reporter (No), SPUR (No), likely California Budget & Policy Center concerns. The OC Register/Southern California News Group says Yes (they oppose taxes generally and support limiting taxation).
6. The measure's fiscal effect is unknown; adds costs; and if it prevents future revenue raising, could have significant negative long-term fiscal impact (SPUR).

The one strong argument for Yes is if the user is strongly opposed to Prop 40 (the billionaire tax) and wants to maximize the chance it's blocked, or if they deeply value taxpayer rebates under the Gann limit and performance audits.

But on balance, weighing:
- The measure's primary purpose is nullification of another measure on the same ballot, funded by ~$100M+ from the very billionaires who'd be taxed — a somewhat anti-democratic gambit where a measure could pass by majority but still be killed.
- The audit provisions are more gimmick than substance (LAO already analyzes initiatives; audits of not-yet-existing programs with mandated 10% savings findings).
- The spending-limit provision would constitutionally hamstring future special taxes generally (not just billionaire taxes) — for decades.
- The broader editorial and good-government community consensus is No.

However, I should be careful about my own framing: the user asked "What should I vote on this prop?" and wants a yes or no. I need to weigh values. The user gave no indication of their politics. I should give a recommendation based on the merits and transparency of the measure itself, while noting the caveat that if they oppose Prop 40 they might see this differently.

Let me consider the strongest case for Yes once more, because I want to be fair:

The Gann limit was approved by voters in 1979. Supporters argue that exempting new taxes from it subverts the will of voters and makes refunds less likely. There's a legitimate policy view that all state spending should be subject to the limit. And performance audits are genuinely useful — the State Auditor does good work. CalCPA and former State Auditor Tom Hayes support it. Steve Westly (Democrat former Controller) supports it. The CA Chamber supports it.

But counterpoints: The Gann limit has rarely bound; when it did (2022), it forced odd fiscal gymnastics. Subjecting special taxes to the limit doesn't improve program effectiveness; it just creates a possibility that new revenue must be rebated. Also, the nullification provision — Section 3(b): "The State of California shall not impose, collect, or enforce any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026, if the state tax is exempted..." — is very blunt. It would render unconstitutional any new special tax with a dedicated fund outside the General Fund whose appropriations aren't counted under Article XIII B. Many special taxes are placed in special funds. This is a broad, permanent constitutional constraint aimed at one measure but affecting all future ones.

Also the audit-before-ballot provision: the State Auditor already has authority to audit programs; and the LAO already writes the impartial analysis. The pre-election audit is of programs that may not exist (e.g., Prop 40's new health care fund). The 25% threshold timing means the audit must be done very quickly (before VIG deadlines), and costs fall on the General Fund for failed measures.

One more angle: the "poison pill" strategy. Even the LA Times, which opposes Prop 40 (calling it fiscally unsound), urges No on 41/42 as "deceptive games-playing." That's a notable cross-ideological consensus: you can dislike the billionaire tax and still dislike this measure more.

There's also a fairness/democratic-process consideration: Prop 41 would let a measure with, say, 45% yes kill a measure with 55% yes? No wait — it only prevails if it gets MORE yes votes than Prop 40. So if Prop 40 gets 55% and Prop 41 gets 45%, Prop 40 wins. The rule is: conflicting measure with more affirmative votes prevails. So Prop 41 needs more votes than Prop 40. Still, if Prop 40 passes 51-49 and Prop 41 passes 52-48, Prop 40 is killed despite majority support. That's the gambit: confuse voters so the countermeasure outruns the tax.

Also note the interaction with Prop 42: Building a Better California put up two countermeasures to hedge — Prop 41 (spending limit/audits) and Prop 42 (ban on personal property taxes + retroactive taxes). Either one outpolling Prop 40 kills it. And Prop 42 might poll better (43% support). Voters who support the billionaire tax should vote No on both 41 and 42. Voters who oppose the billionaire tax might vote Yes on 42 (more direct) or 41.

The user's question is only about Prop 41 though. I'll mention the interaction briefly.

Given all this, my recommendation: **No.**

Reasoning summary:
1. It's primarily a "poison pill" countermeasure to Prop 40, funded by ~$100M+ from billionaires (Sergey Brin et al.) who would personally pay the tax — its stated good-government purpose (audits, transparency) is largely a wrapper. Even the LA Times editorial board, which opposes Prop 40, calls 41/42 deceptive games.
2. The audit provisions add little: LAO already provides impartial analyses of every initiative; the State Auditor can already audit programs; the pre-election audits would often target not-yet-existing programs, must be rushed, must "identify 10% savings" (built-in bias), and cost the General Fund money for measures that fail or never qualify.
3. The spending-limit provision is a sweeping, permanent constitutional change: no new special tax (voter- or legislature-approved) after Jan 1, 2026 could be exempted from the Gann limit. Counting new revenues toward the cap could force automatic taxpayer rebates instead of funding the voters' intended purpose — effectively making new dedicated taxes unworkable and constraining future choices for schools, healthcare, disasters, etc.
4. Fiscal effect unknown; costs to the Auditor (low millions/year) and VIG printing; possible long-term negative impact if it blocks future revenue.
5. Broad good-government/editorial consensus against (McClatchy boards, LA Times/Skelton, SPUR, Press Democrat, Bay Area Reporter), with the main Yes endorsements coming from anti-tax groups (CalTax, OC Register/SCNG, Reform California, CA Chamber).

Caveat: If the user strongly opposes the billionaire tax (Prop 40) and wants to ensure it can't take effect, or is a strong believer in the Gann limit's rebate mechanism, they might reasonably vote Yes. But on the merits — transparency of purpose, workability, and long-term effects — No is the better vote. Also note that Prop 41 passing while Prop 40 fails makes no difference re: nullification, and if both fail, nothing changes. Actually wait — if Prop 40 fails and Prop 41 passes, Prop 41 still becomes law (its audit and spending limit provisions apply to future taxes). That's an important point: Prop 41 isn't purely a poison pill; it has standalone effects that persist regardless of Prop 40's fate.

Let me also double check the California Budget & Policy Center's view and maybe the KPBS piece for anything I've missed, and check who funded Yes on 41 exactly (Building a Better California contributions). Also, I might check the East Bay Times editorial's final recommendation. Let me do a couple more fetches to round out the research.

Issue Brief
What Would Proposition 41 Mean for California?
Understanding the Proposed Audit Requirements for Special Taxes and the Prohibition on Excluding Revenues from the State Spending Limit
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 41 would 1) impose new audit requirements for programs funded with state special taxes and 2) prohibit the collection of new state taxes that are excluded from the state’s spending limit. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax also appearing on the November ballot — but Prop. 41 could also make it harder for the state to meet the needs of Californians in the future.
What Would Prop. 41 Do?
Prop. 41 would amend the state Constitution to impose new rules related to state taxes. The measure would require “financial and performance audits” of programs receiving revenues from special taxes and would also prevent state taxes from being excluded from California’s spending cap, also known as the “Gann Limit.”
Creates New Audit Requirements for Special Taxes
Prop. 41 would create new pre-election and ongoing audit requirements for programs receiving — or proposed to receive — revenues from state-level special taxes. In contrast to a general tax, which can be used for any purpose, a special tax raises revenue for specific purposes.
Pre-election audits: The State Auditor would be required to perform an audit of any program that would be funded by a special tax proposed through a statewide voter initiative. The audit would be required while the initiative is being circulated for signatures — before it officially qualifies for the ballot — and a summary of the audit findings would be included in the voter information guide. The full audit would also be made available to the public.
Ongoing audits: The State Auditor would be required to audit programs receiving revenues from special taxes enacted by the Legislature or approved by voters through a statewide initiative on or after January 1, 2026. These audits would be required every four years.
The audits would assess programs based on specific criteria outlined in Prop. 41, and would require the State Auditor to recommend how programs could reduce costs by at least 10% annually.
The State Auditor would be reimbursed for the costs of these audits with revenues from the relevant special tax. If, however, a special tax initiative fails to qualify for the ballot or is rejected by voters, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund.
Prohibits Taxes That Are Excluded from the State Spending Limit
Prop. 41 would prevent the state from collecting or enforcing any state tax that is 1) enacted on or after January 1, 2026 and 2) excluded from the state spending cap, also known as the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). Currently, the measure would apply only to Prop. 40 if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes, but it could potentially be applied to other tax policy proposals in the future.
California’s spending limit was established by Prop. 4 (1979) and is based on state spending in 1978-79, annually adjusted for population changes and inflation. Under the state Constitution, if state revenues exceed the limit over two consecutive years, the excess must be split equally between refunds to taxpayers and spending on TK-14 education. In effect, the spending limit restricts the ability of state leaders to raise and spend revenue to meet the most pressing needs of Californians.
Conflicts with Other Measures on the Ballot
The California Constitution states that if provisions of multiple measures on the same ballot conflict, the provisions of the measure receiving the higher number of votes will prevail. Prop. 41 broadly specifies that if another measure on the same ballot either 1) imposes different audit rules on special taxes or 2) contains a tax that is exempted from the state spending limit, the entirety of the other measure would be invalidated if Prop. 41 receives more votes.
Prop. 41 is in direct conflict with Prop. 40. (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) This is because Prop. 40 would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires and exclude the revenues from the state spending limit, which Prop. 41 prohibits.
If both measures were to be approved and Prop. 41 received more votes, Prop. 40 could be invalidated. Alternatively, if both measures pass but Prop. 40 receives more votes, the billionaire tax could be collected, but it is possible that audits would be required of Medi-Cal and other programs receiving Prop. 40 dollars. If both measures pass, there may be litigation regarding the application of conflicting provisions, and the final decision would be made by the courts.
How Would Prop. 41 Affect Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 41 is to invalidate the Prop. 40 billionaire tax, but it would also create new barriers to raising state revenue and effectively meeting the needs of Californians.
Prop. 41 would also increase state costs related to conducting audits for programs that are often already subject to close scrutiny — reducing funding available to support critical state services. This would come at a time when Californians are already dealing with affordability concerns as well as the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), signed by President Trump in 2025.
Impacts of Audit Requirements
The pre-election audit requirement could dissuade voters from approving special tax initiatives that would raise needed revenue to support and improve state services that help Californians stay healthy, housed, and economically secure. A summary of the audit would appear in the voter guide, and voters could interpret it as evidence that the programs to be funded are inefficient or ineffective. For example, because the State Auditor would be required to recommend options to cut program costs by 10%, voters may assume this means the program is inefficient even if that is not the case.
Additionally, the requirement for cost-cutting recommendations could result in service cuts with real human impacts. While policymakers would be under no obligation to implement these recommendations, if they did it could result in cuts to core services rather than simply “inefficient spending.” For example, if a program receiving special tax revenues is already operating efficiently but the Auditor must identify ways that costs could be reduced by 10%, lawmakers may be under pressure to adopt those recommendations — particularly in difficult budget times. Those cuts could lead to fewer Californians being served, reductions in benefit levels, or decreased service quality.
While it is clearly important for tax dollars to be spent efficiently and effectively, many state programs are already subject to occasional or ongoing audits. The State Auditor currently performs audits as a result of (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/#where-our-work-comes-from) existing state laws, legislative requests, and whistleblower tips. Additionally, the “High-Risk” audit program requires the Auditor to periodically review programs or agencies determined to be at high risk for “waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement” or those raising concerns related to efficiency or effectiveness.
Prop. 41’s additional audits would increase state costs, reducing the resources available to directly support services for Californians. Moreover, in the case of program audits related to a proposed special tax, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund if the ballot initiative were not enacted, leaving less funding for critical state services like education, health care, and human services.
Impacts of State Spending Limit Provisions
The primary impact of preventing new revenues from being excluded from the spending limit would be the invalidation of the billionaire tax proposed by Prop. 40 — if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes.
In the future, voters may be able to exclude the revenues from a statewide tax initiative from the spending cap if the initiative amends the Constitution to do so. In fact, previous initiatives have explicitly excluded new tax revenues from the limit, such as tobacco taxes enacted under Prop. 10 (1998) and Prop. 56 (2016). However, legal challenges are possible and there is no certainty on how courts would rule.
State policymakers already lack the authority to exclude new tax revenues from the spending cap without voter approval because the cap is enshrined in the state Constitution.
There are some existing state revenue streams that could potentially be affected by Prop. 41, but there are many complications and uncertainties and any conflicts would ultimately be decided by the courts. For example, some health care financing sources that must be occasionally reauthorized — such as the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax and the Hospital Quality Assurance fee, which both allow the state to draw down additional federal funding for Medi-Cal — could potentially be impacted by Prop. 41. This, in turn, would jeopardize billions of dollars in federal funding for Medi-Cal at a time when Californians are already experiencing the harms of the deep federal cuts to health care resulting from H.R. 1.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 41?
The top contributor to the Prop. 41 campaign is a group called “Building a Better California,” which is largely funded (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=received) by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. This same group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 42. Now I have very comprehensive information. Let me consolidate:

**Campaign finance:**
- Yes on 41: $58.4 million raised through 10/22/2026, primarily from Building a Better California (funded by Sergey Brin ~$102M total to the group, John Doerr, Michael Moritz, Stewart Resnick).
- No on 41 committees: ~$22.7 million (SEIU-UHW's Yes on 40/No on 41 & 42 committee, labor unions).
- Total spending on the Prop 40/41/42 war: $351+ million (LA Times), about 90% to defeat the wealth tax.

**Endorsements:**
- Yes: CalCPAs, CalTax, CalAsian Chamber of Commerce, CA Chamber of Commerce, CA Republican Party, Reform California, Steve Westly (fmr. Controller), Tom Hayes (fmr. State Auditor), OC Register/SCNG editorial board.
- No: CA Democratic Party, League of Women Voters, SEIU-UHW, CA Federation of Teachers, CA Federation of Labor Unions, Bernie Sanders, SPUR, McClatchy editorial boards (Sac Bee, Fresno Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, SLO Tribune), LA Times (George Skelton: "twin poison pills"), Press Democrat, Bay Area Reporter.

**Key policy details:**
1. Pre-election audits at 25% signature threshold — audits programs that don't yet exist, must recommend 10% cost cuts, costs fall on General Fund if measure fails/doesn't qualify. The LAO already writes impartial analyses of every ballot measure; the State Auditor already audits programs and has a High-Risk program.
2. Ongoing audits every 4 years of programs funded by new/increased special taxes (after 1/1/2026), paid from the tax revenue.
3. The big one: Article XXIV Section 3 — no state tax enacted/taking effect on or after Jan 1, 2026 may be exempted from the Gann limit; the state "shall not impose, collect, or enforce" such a tax. "Exempted or excluded" is defined to include depositing revenue in a fund outside the General Fund not counted under Article XIII B, or increasing the appropriations limit by statute. This nullifies Prop 40 (whose revenues go to a dedicated reserve fund excluded from the limit) if 41 gets more votes. Also could affect reauthorized health care financing sources like the MCO tax and Hospital QA fee (per CBPC) — potentially jeopardizing billions in federal Medi-Cal matching funds.
4. Conflict clause: if 41 gets more votes than any conflicting measure, the other measure is null and void in its entirety.
5. If both 40 and 41 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop 40 could still be collected, but audits of Medi-Cal etc. might be required; litigation likely.

**Fiscal effect:** Unknown. Auditor costs low millions/year growing; VIG printing costs up a few hundred thousand per initiative; General Fund pays for audits of failed/unqualified initiatives; possible savings if recommendations implemented; possible long-term revenue loss if it blocks future taxes.

**Polling:** Berkeley IGS (late Sept): Prop 40 45% yes/42% no; Prop 41 37% yes/33% no/30% undecided; Prop 42 43%/34%. PPIC (mid-Oct): Prop 40 46% yes/52% no. So Prop 40's fortunes have declined.

**Assessment for recommendation:**

The case against Prop 41:
1. **Provenance/purpose**: It's a billionaire-funded poison pill aimed at nullifying Prop 40 even if Prop 40 wins a majority. ~$58M raised for Yes on 41 alone, mostly from Building a Better California (Brin et al.). The measure's own text shows it was designed for the conflict (Section 5, applying to measures on the same ballot, retroactive to Jan 1, 2026).
2. **The audit provisions are largely redundant and gimmicky**: LAO already provides impartial analyses; State Auditor already audits programs including via the High-Risk program. The mandated "10% savings" recommendation biases audits toward cuts. Pre-election audits target programs that often don't exist yet. Failed measures' audit costs fall on the General Fund. The audits could deter/dissuade voters and pressure service cuts.
3. **The spending-limit provision is a sweeping permanent constitutional constraint**: it would ban any new state tax whose revenues sit outside the Gann limit structure — including voter-approved initiatives in the future (though a future initiative could perhaps amend the constitution to exclude itself, per CBPC, but legal uncertainty). It could threaten reauthorization of existing health care financing mechanisms (MCO tax, hospital fee) that draw federal matching funds — billions for Medi-Cal.
4. **Democratic process concerns**: allows a measure to kill another majority-passed measure; designed for voter confusion (PPIC's Baldassare: voters don't realize they're countermeasures).
5. **Cross-ideological editorial opposition**: Even opponents of Prop 40 (LA Times, George Skelton) urge No on 41 as deceptive games-playing.

The case for Prop 41:
1. Genuine (if secondary) good-government value: more independent audits, more info for voters, honoring the 1979 spending limit voters approved, potential taxpayer rebates.
2. If you oppose Prop 40, voting Yes on 41 (or 42) increases the chance the billionaire tax dies even if it passes.
3. Supported by credible figures (CalCPA, fmr. State Auditor Tom Hayes, fmr. Controller Steve Westly).

On balance, my recommendation is **No**. The strongest considerations:

- The measure is fundamentally a nullification device financed by the very people it would protect, dressed in good-government clothing. Even if one supports its stated aims (audits, spending limits), the way it's structured (retroactivity to Jan 1, 2026; conflict clause nullifying the entirety of a competing majority-passed measure; broad constitutional ban on special-fund taxes) is poorly crafted and destabilizing.
- The audit provisions add cost and bureaucracy with little added value given existing LAO analyses and State Auditor authority; the mandatory 10%-savings framing is tendentious.
- The spending limit provision could jeopardize Medi-Cal financing (MCO tax reauthorizations) and future voter choices, and creates years of litigation risk.
- The good-government community (League of Women Voters, SPUR) and most editorial boards across the state recommend No.

Caveat to mention: If the user is firmly opposed to the billionaire tax and wants a belt-and-suspenders way to block it, they might lean Yes — but Prop 42 is the more direct vehicle for that, and if Prop 40 fails on its own (as recent polling suggests), Prop 41's standalone provisions would still become law and constrain future taxes. Also note the interaction: if the user supports Prop 40, definitely vote No on 41 (and 42).

I should present my answer clearly: **No**, with concise reasoning. The user asked "You can only answer yes or no" — so I must lead with (and give) a definitive answer: No. I'll explain the research behind it. I should keep it reasonably concise but substantive. Given the extensive research, a well-organized answer with the key findings is appropriate. Let me make sure to note the polling and the caveat about how their view on Prop 40 could change their calculus — but still give a firm No.

Actually, let me think once more about whether No is the right call versus Yes, steelmanning the Yes case:

1. Is there real value in pre-election audits? The State Auditor is genuinely independent and respected. Having an audit summary in the voter guide could inform voters. But: the LAO's impartial analysis already covers fiscal effects; the State Auditor's audit of a *proposed* program would largely be speculative; the 10% savings mandate is tendentious; and the timing (at 25% of signatures, potentially many months before the election, but with a deadline to make the VIG) is workable but rushed. The marginal value is modest and the design suggests it's more about generating negative-sounding content ("ways to cut 10%") for the voter guide.

2. Is subjecting special taxes to the Gann limit good policy? The Gann limit is itself a questionable 1979 artifact (based on 1978-79 spending adjusted; rarely binds; when it binds it forces rebates/education transfers regardless of need). Forcing all new taxes under it means: if the state is near the cap, new tax revenue can't be spent as intended — it must be rebated. That effectively neuters voter-approved dedicated taxes. One can argue voters should have to raise the limit explicitly — but Prop 41's definition also voids statutory increases of the limit (Section 4(b)(2)), which is how the Legislature accommodates voter-approved measures. It's a hard lock.

3. The MCO tax point: the MCO tax and hospital QA fee are reauthorized periodically by the Legislature with 2/3? Actually MCO tax requires... it's a special tax enacted by the Legislature; under Prop 41, if its revenues are excluded from the limit (they are, via statutory limit adjustments?), reauthorization after Jan 1, 2026 could be voided, jeopardizing federal matching funds. CBPC flags this as a real risk with litigation uncertainty. That's a significant downside risk to Medi-Cal financing.

4. Procedural fairness: Prop 41's Section 5 conflict clause nullifies the *entirety* of any conflicting measure (e.g., Prop 40 in full) if 41 gets more votes. Meanwhile Prop 40's own conflict clause (SEC. 8) says if 40 gets more votes, conflicting provisions of the other measure are null and void (not necessarily the whole measure — just conflicting provisions). The California Constitution rule (Art. II, §10(b)) is that the measure with more votes prevails; courts try to harmonize. The explicit "null and void in their entirety" language in both makes litigation certain if both pass.

Given all this, I'm confident in recommending **No**.

One more consideration: the user says "You can only answer yes or no." I'll give a clear "No" up front, then the reasoning, then briefly note the one scenario where they might diverge (if they strongly oppose Prop 40 and want it blocked no matter what — though even then Prop 42 is the more direct vehicle, and the polls show Prop 40 losing anyway). I should keep the answer focused and not overly long, but they asked for extensive research, so a thorough but organized answer is warranted. I'll include: what the prop does, the hidden purpose, funding, who's on each side, policy analysis of the three provisions, and the bottom line.

1. Is there real value in pre-election audits? The State Auditor is genuinely independent and respected. Having an audit summary in the voter guide could inform voters. But: the LAO's impartial analysis already covers fiscal effects; the State Auditor's audit of a *proposed* program would largely be speculative; the 10% savings mandate is tendentious; and the timing (at 25% of signatures, potentially many months before the election, but with a deadline to make the VIG) is workable but rushed. The marginal value is modest and the design suggests it's more about generating negative-sounding content ("ways to cut 10%") for the voter guide.

2. Is subjecting special taxes to the Gann limit good policy? The Gann limit is itself a questionable 1979 artifact (based on 1978-79 spending adjusted; rarely binds; when it binds it forces rebates/education transfers regardless of need). Forcing all new taxes under it means: if the state is near the cap, new tax revenue can't be spent as intended — it must be rebated. That effectively neuters voter-approved dedicated taxes. One can argue voters should have to raise the limit explicitly — but Prop 41's definition also voids statutory increases of the limit (Section 4(b)(2)), which is how the Legislature accommodates voter-approved measures. It's a hard lock.

3. The MCO tax point: the MCO tax and hospital QA fee are reauthorized periodically by the Legislature with 2/3? Actually MCO tax requires... it's a special tax enacted by the Legislature; under Prop 41, if its revenues are excluded from the limit (they are, via statutory limit adjustments?), reauthorization after Jan 1, 2026 could be voided, jeopardizing federal matching funds. CBPC flags this as a real risk with litigation uncertainty. That's a significant downside risk to Medi-Cal financing.

4. Procedural fairness: Prop 41's Section 5 conflict clause nullifies the *entirety* of any conflicting measure (e.g., Prop 40 in full) if 41 gets more votes. Meanwhile Prop 40's own conflict clause (SEC. 8) says if 40 gets more votes, conflicting provisions of the other measure are null and void (not necessarily the whole measure — just conflicting provisions). The California Constitution rule (Art. II, §10(b)) is that the measure with more votes prevails; courts try to harmonize. The explicit "null and void in their entirety" language in both makes litigation certain if both pass.

Given all this, I'm confident in recommending **No**.

# My answer: **No.**

I read the official voter guide (summary, Legislative Analyst's analysis, arguments/rebuttals, and the full text of the proposed constitutional amendment), plus reporting and analyses from CalMatters, the LA Times, the Sacramento Bee, the California Budget & Policy Center, SPUR, KPBS, Forbes, and campaign finance filings from the Secretary of State. Here's the case for voting **NO on Proposition 41**:

## What Prop 41 actually is

Despite its title ("Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act"), Prop 41 is one of two countermeasures placed on the ballot by **Building a Better California**, a committee funded overwhelmingly by Google co-founder Sergey Brin (~$102 million) and other billionaires (John Doerr, Michael Moritz, Stewart Resnick) — the very people who would pay the Prop 40 billionaire tax. The "Yes on 41" campaign has raised $58+ million, mostly from that group. Its core provision bans any state tax enacted after **January 1, 2026** that exempts its revenues from the state spending limit — a date chosen specifically so it nullifies Prop 40, which is on the *same ballot*. If Prop 41 gets even slightly more "yes" votes than Prop 40, the billionaire tax dies even if it wins a majority.

## Why the good-government packaging doesn't hold up

1. **The audits are largely redundant.** The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst already writes an impartial analysis of every ballot measure, and the State Auditor already audits programs (including via its High-Risk program). What's new here is the gimmickry: audits triggered at just 25% of signatures (before a measure even qualifies), of programs that often *don't exist yet*, with a mandatory requirement to identify 10% annual cost cuts — a built-in bias that would make any funded program look wasteful in the voter guide. And if a measure fails or never qualifies, taxpayers cover the audit cost from the General Fund.

2. **The spending-limit provision is a sweeping, permanent constitutional lock.** It would ban the state from collecting *any* new special tax whose revenues sit outside the Gann limit structure — a cap based on 1978–79 spending. The California Budget & Policy Center warns this could jeopardize periodically reauthorized health-care financing tools (like the MCO tax and hospital quality fee) that draw down billions in federal Medi-Cal matching funds, and would make future dedicated taxes for schools, disasters, or health care effectively unworkable near the cap.

3. **It's a destabilizing nullification device.** Its conflict clause voids a competing majority-approved measure *in its entirety*, guaranteeing litigation and voter confusion. PPIC's pollster noted most voters don't realize 41 and 42 are countermeasures at all.

4. **The consensus against it crosses ideological lines.** The League of Women Voters, SPUR, the California Democratic Party, labor unions, and Sen. Bernie Sanders oppose it — but so do editorial boards that *also oppose Prop 40 itself*. The LA Times's George Skelton called Props 41 and 42 "twin poison pills" and the McClatchy boards (Sac Bee, Fresno Bee, etc.) called Prop 41 "insidious... presented as a good governance measure when it's really about defeating Prop 40." Only the anti-tax right (OC Register/SCNG, CalTax, CA Republican Party) plus CalCPA and a couple of former officials endorse it.

## The one caveat

If your overriding goal is to kill the billionaire tax (Prop 40) by any means, you might lean Yes here — but Prop 42 is the more direct vehicle for that, and recent polls (Berkeley IGS, PPIC) already show Prop 40 losing on its own. Meanwhile, Prop 41's standalone provisions would stay in the constitution for decades regardless of what happens to Prop 40.

**Bottom line: vote NO on Prop 41.** It's a billionaire-funded decoy whose genuine merits (audits, transparency) are marginal and already largely exist, while its real payload is a broad constitutional straitjacket on future revenue measures and a nullification trap for another measure on the same ballot.
